title: Saudi Shuts East-West Pipeline After Iraq-Launched Drone Strike; IEA Cuts 2026 Supply Outlook Again
subhead: Saudi Arabia suspended its East-West export pipeline — the kingdom's main bypass around a blocked Strait of Hormuz — after drones launched from Iraq hit pumping infrastructure, while the IEA cut another 1.4 million bpd from its 2026 supply outlook and pushed Gulf flow recovery into 2027.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia Shuts East-West Pipeline After Iraq-Launched Drone Attack
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia suspended operations on its East-West crude pipeline — the artery that reroutes roughly 5 million bpd toward Yanbu on the Red Sea, bypassing a stricken Strait of Hormuz — after it was hit by drones launched from Iraq. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the pipeline was targeted in the Riyadh and Medina areas by 'several drones originating from Iraq,' causing injuries and material damage, per Al Jazeera. A Saudi Energy Ministry official told the state news agency SPA the pipeline was stopped 'as a precaution.'

The attack's origin is contested at the margins. One U.S. official told CNN the strike involved drones from Iraq, and satellite imagery obtained by CNN showed fire damage at a pumping station near Al Mesba'ah and smoke at another near Al Dhekra. Iraq, for its part, condemned the attack and — after investigations — dismissed a military commander who led operations in Maysan province, with Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordering an inquiry into the Maysan Operations Command.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the first confirmed shutdown of Saudi Arabia's principal Hormuz bypass route, targeting the infrastructure Riyadh has leaned on since the strait closed. The pipeline carries roughly a third of Saudi export capacity and repairs, even to pumping stations, take time — a direct hit on the kingdom's remaining export channel.

sections.heading: Riyadh's Restraint Marks a Shift in Gulf Diplomacy
sections.body:
Equally notable is what Saudi Arabia did not do. The Foreign Ministry said Riyadh would not retaliate for now, at the request of Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, while reserving 'the right to take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty, security and critical facilities.' Iraq said it 'appreciates' Riyadh's move, and the Gulf Cooperation Council's secretary-general, Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, called the attack 'a dangerous escalation and an unacceptable threat to the security of the Kingdom,' per Al Jazeera.

The restraint comes as Saudi energy infrastructure faces mounting pressure from several directions: Houthi attacks along the Red Sea coast, strikes in the kingdom's south that the Energy Ministry confirmed earlier this week, and now a drone assault traced to Iraqi territory — the same provenance Riyadh cited for July attacks on eastern facilities.
sections.whyItMatters: Saudi choosing not to strike back at Iraq — even on a pipeline it depends on — signals Riyadh is managing escalation carefully while at war across multiple fronts. But it also invites the question of how many more hits the kingdom's infrastructure can absorb before restraint becomes unsustainable.

sections.heading: IEA Slashes 2026 Supply Outlook Again, Pushes Gulf Recovery to 2027
sections.body:
The International Energy Agency cut another 1.4 million bpd from its 2026 global oil supply outlook in a report released Friday, now seeing output fall 5.7 million bpd (~6%) this year versus the 4.3-million-bpd decline forecast a month ago, according to an IEA report cited by OilPrice.com. It no longer expects normal Gulf flows to return this year, shifting recovery into 2027.

The numbers are stark: global oil stocks fell at a 3.1 million bpd rate in August, leaving inventories at 7.8 billion barrels, lowest since 2023. Saudi crude supply plunged 2.3 million bpd in August to about 6 million bpd — its lowest in more than three decades — and OPEC+ production fell 1.8 million bpd to 38.8 million bpd. The IEA now expects global consumption to contract 2.5 million bpd this year, up from the 1.6-million-bpd contraction it forecast in August, as record fuel prices destroy demand.

There is a notable gap with OPEC. The IEA's 2026 demand call now sits nearly 2.9 million bpd below OPEC's, which still sees consumption growing 380,000 bpd this year. The two forecasters converge for 2027, seeing demand growth of 2.6 and 2.36 million bpd respectively.
sections.whyItMatters: The IEA is now effectively modeling a deep, sustained supply shock, not a temporary disruption — and it is simultaneously cutting supply and demand forecasts, acknowledging a shortage severe enough to destroy consumption. That divergence with OPEC reflects genuinely different reads on whether this is a demand-led or supply-led contraction.

sections.heading: Hormuz Traffic in Single Digits as Houthis Take the Whole Red Sea Coast
sections.body:
Ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz slumped to single digits Thursday — just seven vessels in 24 hours, two outbound and five inbound, versus a 10-day average of 15 — per Kpler data cited by Reuters and OilPrice.com. Dark transits (ships with AIS switched off) are believed much higher, but tracked volumes exiting the strait remain roughly half of pre-war levels.

The chokepoint squeeze is compounding on the other side of Arabia. Houthi forces captured the whole of Yemen's Red Sea coastline, reaching Bab al-Mandeb itself, after seizing the port city of Mocha on Thursday — gains Al Jazeera reports analysts call the most significant regional development since the U.S.-Israel war on Iran began in February. Saudi Arabia, already leaning on the Red Sea for exports since Hormuz closed, now faces a Red Sea coast under Houthi control; the group declared a blockade of Saudi-flagged ships earlier this year.
sections.whyItMatters: The twin chokepoints — Hormuz throttled and Bab el-Mandeb now effectively hostile — together explain why Saudi's East-West pipeline matters so much: it is the only major artery still connecting Saudi export volumes to open water, and it was just struck.

sections.heading: The Refining Crunch: White House Eyes Defense Production Act as Diesel Tops $6
sections.body:
The White House is considering using the Defense Production Act to add U.S. refining capacity, with American refineries running at 98% utilization and U.S. diesel prices above $6 per gallon for the first time, Reuters reported. The idea was discussed during President Donald Trump's recent meeting with nearly a dozen refiners; no decision has been made. Refiners told officials federal money would produce more barrels faster by expanding existing plants rather than building new ones.

The bottleneck is global, not just American. Phillips 66 estimated roughly 7 million bpd of refining capacity was offline in Asia and the Middle East, with another 1.4 million bpd unavailable in Russia. U.S. diesel inventories sit 13% below their five-year average. A possible test case: America First Refining's planned 168,000-bpd Brownsville, Texas refinery — the first new U.S. refinery in nearly 50 years — is unclear for DPA funding, per Reuters.
sections.whyItMatters: The war has exposed that the world's bottleneck is no longer just crude molecules, but the ability to turn them into diesel and other fuels. Using a Cold War-era defense tool to expand refining capacity signals the shortage has moved from market problem to national-security problem in Washington's view.

sections.heading: China Restocks: Imports Hold at 7.2 Million Bpd as Buying Recovers
sections.body:
China is on track to import about 7.2 million bpd of crude in September, roughly flat with August and extending a recovery from June's decade-low of 7.1 million bpd, per Kpler tracking cited by Nikkei Asia and OilPrice.com. August imports rose 6.2% month on month to 8.93 million bpd on customs data, with refiners turning to non-Middle Eastern supply and boosting Russian ESPO buying and even Argentine barrels.

The September cargoes were largely bought while prices were in the $80s, before crude jumped back above $100. Beijing, having stockpiled roughly 1.4 billion barrels before the war, cut imports sharply at the peak of the crisis and is now re-entering the market — a signal that feeds upward pressure on prices as the IEA warns supply is falling faster than demand.
sections.whyItMatters: China's re-entry is the clearest signal yet that the world's largest importer judges this supply shock as survivable at current prices — either because it has enough reserves to buy opportunistically, or because alternative, non-Middle-East supply is proving workable. Either way, it is removing the demand-side cushion that had been moderating prices.

sections.heading: LNG and the Broader Gas Shock
sections.body:
Away from crude, the war has upended global gas markets. Commodity analysts — Rystad Energy, Kpler, ICIS, and S&P Global — have cut their LNG supply outlooks by some 35 million tons, driven by force majeure on Qatar's LNG facilities and delays to Qatar's North Field expansion and ADNOC's Ruwais project, Reuters reported. Kpler's Laura Page said the market rebalances 'primarily through higher prices and demand destruction in South Asia,' with 'sustained $20+ levels' seen likely through summer for Asia, where LNG prices have surged 143% since the war began. Rystad estimates the total cost of repairing oil and gas infrastructure damaged so far at $25 billion, with Qatari and Iranian gas infrastructure the most damaged.

As in oil, the cushion is thin: U.S. LNG export plants are at capacity and much output is tied to long-term contracts, so U.S. gas cannot quickly fill the gap. Poorer Asian buyers are switching back to coal, while China has insulated itself via Power of Siberia pipeline volumes and Novatek's Arctic LNG 2, one Chinese gas trader told Reuters.
sections.whyItMatters: The LNG story mirrors crude but with a sharper regional edge: South Asia absorbs the pain through demand destruction and coal backsliding, while China — protected by Russian pipeline and Arctic LNG supply — sits out the worst of it. That is a structural realignment in global gas leverage in Asia's most populous markets.

sections.heading: Oil Markets: Brent ~$104 After a Week Above $100
sections.body: Brent held near $104.6 early Friday, down about 2.8% on the day but closing a trading week above the $100 mark for the first time since May, per OilPrice.com price data. Gulf-grade Murban traded at a far larger premium near $119.5, highlighting how severely Gulf crude specifically is being repriced. ING strategists Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey wrote that 'oil's resilience reflects a market now repricing both the duration and severity of the conflict,' and Energy Aspects argues the market has reached an inflection point as inventory drawdowns accelerate.
sections.whyItMatters: The intraday dip obscures the broader signal: oil has settled structurally above $100 with crude, diesel, and Gulf-light-crude all at war premia. With the IEA cutting supply into 2027 and Saudi's export artery now struck, the market's baseline assumption is a long, expensive shortage rather than a quick fix.

bottomLine: The defining development of the day is Saudi Arabia's shutdown of its East-West pipeline after a drone attack traced to Iraq — the first confirmed strike on the kingdom's principal Hormuz-bypass export artery, carried on top of a Houthi-held Red Sea coast, Hormuz traffic in single digits, and an IEA that has slashed 5.7 million bpd out of 2026 supply with Gulf recovery pushed to 2027. Riyadh's decision not to retaliate, at Baghdad's request, shows Gulf capitals trying to manage escalation even as their export infrastructure comes under successive attack. With Brent above $100, diesel over $6 a gallon in the U.S., and Washington weighing the Defense Production Act to add refining capacity, the market is pricing a long, expensive shortage — and China's cautious re-entry into crude buying suggests the world's largest importer is betting it can ride it out.
sources: OilPrice.com (Tom Kool, Julianne Geiger, Tsvetana Paraskova, Irina Slav), Al Jazeera, CNN, Reuters, SPA, Nikkei Asia, Kpler, IEA, Energy Aspects, ING (Warren Patterson, Ewa Manthey), Rystad Energy
